title: Islip: Colonial Estates and Continuing Native Rights
summary: William Nicoll’s 1683 agreement retained Native residence, planting and fishing rights on land he had not developed. English patents strengthened private estate claims, but Native residents remained. Islip’s separate estates show why a deed, a colonial patent and a town are different parts of land-loss history.

why_this_matters: The English deed itself retained Native rights, while later patents strengthened a private estate. Reading those records alongside evidence of Native residents in 1798 challenges the idea that paper ownership meant people or their relationships with the land had vanished.

history_title: Agreements, English authority and continuing Native presence
history_content:
Land agreements did not mean Native people disappeared

The November 29, 1683 agreement between Winnaquaheagh and William Nicoll contains two kinds of rights. Its English legal language records a land claim for Nicoll and his successors. It also permits Winnaquaheagh and his heirs to live, plant, hunt, fowl and fish on portions Nicoll had not farmed or improved. That condition matters: development could reduce the places where those recorded rights applied. The deed does not establish what every participant understood. East of Islip: An Early History, printed pp. 4

A deed, a patent and a town were separate steps

The Town of Islip's historical notes identify English colonial governor Thomas Dongan as confirming Nicoll's first tract on December 5, 1684, requiring an annual payment to the Crown. Other estates belonged to Andrew Gibb, Stephen Van Cortlandt, Richard and Thomas Willets, and John Mowbray. Islip was assembled from separate claims, rather than one agreement covering today's town. Description of the Town of Islip, January 11, 1798, printed pp. 14

How English authority enlarged a private claim

On September 20, 1697, Governor Benjamin Fletcher issued another patent to William Nicoll in the name of King William III. Its terms included a tract of land and Raconchony Pond, along with waterways, meadows, fishing, hunting, resources and jurisdiction. It granted these interests to Nicoll and his successors under an English form of tenure tied to the royal manor of East Greenwich in Kent. This was an overseas government's legal framework being applied to an inhabited Native landscape. Long Island Colonial Patents, printed pp. 85–86

The sequence matters. A Native agreement, a royal patent and a later town boundary are different records of power. The patent's language of permanent inheritance describes what the colonial government claimed to grant; it cannot by itself tell us that every Native owner consented, or that all earlier access rights ended. Nor does one later patent establish the boundaries of the first 1683 transaction. East of Islip: An Early History, printed pp. 4; Long Island Colonial Patents, printed pp. 85–86

Native presence after the patents

In January 1798, town supervisor Nathaniel Conklin recorded Native residents in Islip. His account groups Native, mixed-ancestry and free Black residents together across 25 dwellings; it does not provide a separate Native household count. Colonial landholding had not made Native people disappear. Description of the Town of Islip, January 11, 1798, printed pp. 5–11
whereintheworld_content: This shaded area follows the modern Islip mainland, from West Islip toward Bayport on Long Island's South Shore. It brings together places affected by separate colonial estates; it is not Nicoll's 1683 deed boundary or a claim that the entire area changed hands at once. Great South Bay, Fire Island and detached islands are omitted. Today's town lines provide orientation, not evidence of Native consent. NYS Civil Boundaries: Towns
